intro: A weight falls in a Manchester cellar and a can of water grows warmer by a fraction of a degree. A strip of card splits a sunbeam and paints stripes of darkness on a wall. A compass needle twitches when a wire beside it carries current. None of these looked important at the time. Each turned out to be a door into one of the deepest ideas in physics: that energy is conserved and flows only downhill, that light and sound are waves that add and cancel, and that electricity and magnetism are two faces of one thing.

This unit follows those doors. The first chapter tracks energy from a lifted backpack to a spinning generator: work and power, springs and swings, heat and temperature, the laws of thermodynamics that no engine can escape, and the entropy that gives time its direction. The second chapter follows waves: interference on the site's wave bench, resonance on the drum bench, the Doppler slide of a passing siren, rays through the telescope and the microscope, the puzzle that made light both wave and particle, and the charge, current and induction that let a diamond stylus in a record groove become music from the turntables.

By the end you will be able to explain why a car crash at double the speed does four times the damage, why Lake Michigan keeps Chicago's lakefront cool in May, why no power plant can turn all its heat into electricity, how two beams of light can add up to darkness, why a galaxy's color tells you it is receding, and why a magnet sitting still next to a coil does nothing at all.
bigQuestion: How do energy, waves and fields, which no one can see directly, explain nearly everything we can?

timeline.t: Robert Hooke publishes drawings made with a microscope and, within a decade, the law of springs.
Isaac Newton's Opticks argues that light is a stream of particles; the view dominates for a century.
Thomas Young shows the Royal Society that light passing both sides of a card makes bright and dark fringes.
Hans Christian Ørsted sees a compass needle turn beside a current-carrying wire.
Sadi Carnot works out the maximum efficiency of any heat engine.
Michael Faraday finds that a changing magnetic field induces a current: the generator is born.
Christian Doppler explains why a moving source's waves shift in pitch or color.
James Joule publishes the mechanical equivalent of heat from his paddle-wheel experiments.
Rudolf Clausius names entropy and states that the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
James Clerk Maxwell's equations predict electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light.
Albert Einstein explains the photoelectric effect with light quanta, later called photons.
Enrico Fermi's team in Chicago runs the first controlled nuclear chain reaction.

the rate of energy transfer, in watts (joules per second)

a measure of how spread out energy is, counting the arrangements that match what you see
the adding and canceling of overlapping waves
a large response when an object is pushed at one of its natural frequencies

test.q: Joule's paddle-wheel experiment was important because it showed that:
choices: mechanical work and heat are the same kind of thing, energy
water cannot be warmed without fire
temperature is a form of force
test.why: A fixed amount of work from falling weights always produced a fixed amount of heat, establishing heat as energy.

test.q: A car doubles its speed. To stop it, the brakes must now remove:
test.why: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples the energy.

test.q: A 2000-watt heater runs for 30 minutes. It uses:
A pendulum bob swings back to almost, but not quite, the height it was released from. The small loss is because:
choices: potential energy leaks into the ceiling
air drag and friction turned some energy into heat
test.why: Energy is conserved overall, but a little mechanical energy becomes thermal energy every swing.

test.q: Equal masses of water and iron each absorb 1000 joules. Which warms more, and why?
choices: Iron, because its specific heat is much lower
Water, because it is a liquid
Both the same, since the energy is equal
test.why: Temperature rise is Q divided by m c. Iron's specific heat is about a ninth of water's, so it warms about nine times more.

test.q: A heat engine runs between 600 kelvin and 300 kelvin. Which claimed efficiency is impossible?
test.why: The Carnot limit is 1 minus 300 over 600, or 50 percent. No engine between those temperatures can exceed it.

test.q: Which best explains why total entropy increases?
choices: Energy is used up in every process
Cold objects absorb entropy from hot ones
Spread-out arrangements of energy vastly outnumber concentrated ones
Friction is present in every machine
test.why: Systems drift toward the most numerous microscopic arrangements, which are the spread-out ones.

test.q: Illinois generates about half of its electricity from:
test.why: Illinois has eleven reactors at six plants, more than any other state, supplying roughly half its generated electricity.

test.q: Two speakers play the same steady tone. Walking across the room, a listener hears loud spots and nearly silent spots. The silent spots are where:
choices: the two sound waves arrive half a wavelength out of step and cancel
the sound has been absorbed by the walls
test.why: This is destructive interference: crest meets trough where the path difference is half a wavelength.

test.q: A guitar string's fundamental note fits how much of a wavelength between its fixed ends?
test.why: Both ends are nodes, so the simplest standing wave is a single loop, half a wavelength long.

test.q: A siren's pitch drops the moment an ambulance passes you because:
choices: sound slows down behind the vehicle
the waves are now stretched apart as the source moves away
the air behind the ambulance is thinner
test.why: Once the source recedes, each crest is emitted from farther away, lengthening the wavelength and lowering the frequency.

test.q: Light traveling inside glass hits the glass-to-air surface at a steep angle and does not exit at all. This is:
test.why: Beyond the critical angle, Snell's law has no solution for the exiting ray and all the light reflects back inside.

test.q: Dim ultraviolet light releases electrons from a metal but bright red light does not. This supports the idea that:
choices: light energy comes in packets whose size depends on frequency
red light is absorbed by metal
brightness has no effect on light energy
electrons only respond to ultraviolet color
test.why: Each electron takes energy from one photon. Red photons are below the threshold, and more of them do not help a single electron.

test.q: A 6-volt battery is connected to a 3-ohm resistor. The current is:
test.why: Ohm's law: I = V / R = 6 divided by 3 = 2 amperes.

test.q: A turntable cartridge produces a voltage because:
choices: the record is charged by friction
heat from the stylus drives a current
the stylus moves a magnet or coil, changing the magnetic field through the coil
the motor's electricity flows through the needle
test.why: Electromagnetic induction: the groove wiggles the stylus, the field through the coil changes, and a small voltage copies the groove.

write.prompt: Make a claim: is it accurate to say the world is running out of energy? Use evidence from Joule's experiment, the laws of thermodynamics, engine efficiency and entropy to argue whether the problem is a shortage of energy or something else.
tips: Claim: state clearly whether energy is running out, or whether something else is, in one sentence.
Evidence: use the first law (energy conserved), the Carnot limit on engines, and the second law's rule about entropy and spread-out energy.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence connects to your claim, using the idea of useful versus spread-out energy.
The other side: describe why people commonly say we are running out of energy, and what is true in that worry even if the wording is wrong.
Close with one real example, such as a power plant on an Illinois river or a car engine, that shows your claim in action.
